G. Statistical Analysis
Uncertainty quantification: Patient-level bootstrap confi￾dence intervals (1,000 replicates, seed 42) are the primary
uncertainty quantification throughout this paper [43]. For
the perturbation audit, bootstrap replicates resample patients
(not individual ECGs) with replacement; all ECGs belonging
to a resampled patient are included, preserving the within￾patient correlation structure. ASS is computed on the paired
target-versus-control perturbation effects within each replicate,
maintaining the matched-subject design.
Model comparison: Pairwise model comparisons (ResNet
vs XGBoost Simple, ResNet vs XGBoost Clinical-MVP, XG￾Boost Clinical-MVP vs Simple) were performed per disease
on the shared test set. For AUROC, we used the DeLong
test [44] for paired comparisons on identical test samples.
For F1, we used vectorized paired permutation tests with
5,000 resamples [45]. Two-sided p-values were computed as
the proportion of |permuted ∆F1| ≥ |observed ∆F1|. Holm￾Bonferroni correction was applied to the family of 18 compar￾isons (3 model pairs × 5 diseases + 3 macro-F1). We note that
permutation p-values and DeLong tests operate at the sample
level (n ≈ 69, 500 ECGs from approximately 47,000 unique
patients; mean 1.48 samples/patient); because within-patient
correlations reduce the effective sample size, sample-level tests
may produce optimistic p-values and are reported for com￾pleteness as approximate secondary indicators. Patient-level
bootstrap CIs provide the primary uncertainty quantification.
Multiplicity control for external pathway tests: The
primary external audit tests 15 pre-specified hypotheses of
the form H0 : ASS ≤ 0 (one-sided) under the primary
linear-interpolation operator on PTB-XL fold 10. We apply
the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) pro￾cedure at α = 0.05 to control the expected proportion of false
positives among rejected hypotheses. Bootstrap p-values are
computed as 1−Pr(ASS¿0), where Pr(ASS> 0) is the fraction
of bootstrap replicates with positive ASS. Storey q-values are
reported alongside BH-FDR thresholds (Table XIII).
Cross-dataset feature-space validation: XGBoost models
were also trained on PTB-XL+ 12SL features (783D) using
official PTB-XL patient-level folds (1–8 train, 9 validation
for threshold tuning, 10 test) [18], [33]. Labels were mapped
from SCP-ECG codes to the 5 target diseases using strict
primary diagnostic codes only. For 1AVB contextualization,
a PR>200ms rule baseline was computed using NeuroKit2’s
wavelet-based ECG delineation on the original 500Hz signal;
the continuous PR interval AUROC is compared against
ResNet AUROC via the DeLong test.
IV. RESULTS
A. Baseline Discrimination Establishes the Context for Path￾way Auditing
We first establish the discrimination context for the
matched-control audit. This step is methodological rather than
a primary result: the audit asks whether a functioning classifier
uses disease-consistent signal pathways, and a negative audit
result is interpretable only if the model has learned the disease
label to a nontrivial degree. Otherwise, ASS ≤ 0 could reflect
either absent pathway specificity or classification failure.
The audited raw-signal models generally achieved strong
discrimination on the five-disease panel. ResNet reached AU￾ROC > 0.98 for all five diseases (Table IV), with Micro￾F1= 0.736, and SE-ResNet was statistically indistinguishable
from ResNet. The lightweight Transformer preserved BBB
detection (CRBBB F1 0.805; CLBBB 0.807) but was weaker
on rhythm disorders (SBRAD F1 0.284; AFIB F1 0.585), a
limitation considered when interpreting its rhythm-pathway
audit results. XGBoost with timing-enriched Clinical-MVP
features (110D) provided representation-level context only;
waveform perturbation tiers are assigned only to the three raw￾signal architectures.

D. High Discrimination Does Not Guarantee Medically
Grounded Pathway Use
All five diseases achieve AUROC > 0.98 on ResNet

to discrimination metrics alone: of 15 model-disease pairs, 6
reach Pathway-supported, 1 is Evidence-limited, and 8 are Not
supported (Table XII). This section presents the paper’s central
demonstration that high discrimination can coexist with absent
pathway specificity—the 1AVB matched-control reversal—
and quantifies the discrimination-pathway gap.

Without matched controls, such cases are indistinguishable
from pathway-specific signal use. Every perturbation-based
explanation study that reports target sensitivity without a
matched control is vulnerable to this class of false-positive

expected outcome whenever the model’s decision function
depends on a broader signal region than the clinically expected
one.
2) The Discrimination-Pathway Gap: The contrast between
discrimination and pathway evidence is stark. All five diseases
would be classified as “successful” under a discrimination￾only evaluation (AUROC > 0.98). Yet the per-model audit
reveals three categories:
1) Pathway-supported (6/15 pairs): CRBBB and CLBBB
on all three architectures—positive ASS with CI> 0 on
both datasets, CDDC= 1.0.
2) Evidence-limited (1/15 pairs): SBRAD-ResNet only—
rate-pathway ASS positive on both datasets, but external
CI crosses zero.
3) Not supported (8/15 pairs): 1AVB on all three architec￾tures (matched controls reverse the conclusion); AFIB
atrial-window on all three architectures (ASS negative
under primary operator on both datasets); SBRAD on
SE-ResNet and Transformer (rate-pathway ASS nega￾tive).
A model can be highly accurate without using pathway￾specific signal (1AVB: AUROC 0.985, ASS negative), and a
model can be less accurate while preserving pathway-specific
signal for specific diseases (Transformer: Micro-F1 0.6045,
yet CRBBB/CLBBB Pathway-supported). The audit protocol
thus evaluates models along an axis orthogonal to discrim￾ination, revealing pathway-use patterns invisible to standard
benchmarks.

is not uniform across models—even when discrimination met￾rics are uniformly high. We present findings per architecture to
show what the protocol reveals for each model independently.
ResNet (1.2M params, 1D convolutional): The primary
perturbation-audited instrument. The 1AVB case is the an￾chor demonstration: a large, clinically plausible PR-window
perturbation effect is reversed by matched QRS controls,
yielding negative ASS under all tested operators and on
both datasets—supporting the protocol’s core argument that
target-only perturbation is insufficient for pathway claims.

C. The Limits of Post-Hoc Explainability
The audit protocol also serves as a critique of explanation
evaluation practices that rely on single-region perturbation or
attribution without matched controls. The 1AVB case provides
the clearest demonstration.
A standard perturbation study would test whether perturbing
the PR-target window degrades 1AVB detection. The effect is
large (∆AUROC= −0.226), clinically plausible (the PR in￾terval defines 1AVB), and robust across perturbation methods
(zero-masking, inpainting, Gaussian noise). A conventional ex￾plainability study would stop here and conclude that the model
depends specifically on PR-window information—a publish￾able positive result. But our protocol requires one additional
comparison: matched QRS perturbation. On the same matched
cohort, QRS perturbation is even more disruptive, yielding
negative ASS on both CODE and PTB-XL under all three
tested operators. The operator-comparison battery confirms
this across two architectures: ResNet 1AVB ASS≤ −0.010
for all three operators, SE-ResNet ASS= −0.268 under linear

and the reversal itself is operator-robust and architecture￾consistent.
This is not a pathological edge case. Large target-pathway
effects that appear clinically plausible can coexist with even
larger non-target dependence—and without matched controls,
such cases are indistinguishable from pathway-specific signal
use. The protocol’s matched-control requirement is therefore
not an optional refinement; it is a necessary safeguard against
false-positive pathway claims embedded in existing explain￾ability workflows.
External transfer and operator selection provide two ad￾ditional safeguards. The CRBBB case is instructive: zero￾masking produced the appearance of external pathway failure

and one could cherry-pick the operator that produces the
desired conclusion. The protocol thus combines three design
elements—matched controls, operator selection, and external

false-positive conclusion.
D. Relationship to Prior Work
Most prior ECG explanation studies use saliency maps or
single-region perturbation to show that specific signal regions
influence predictions [7], [20], [21]. Recent work has pro￾posed explanation frameworks for ECG with varying levels
of clinical grounding [3], [24]. The present study differs in
two respects. First, we require target-region perturbations to
be compared against anatomically matched controls—a stricter
criterion that can reveal false-positive pathway claims, as
the 1AVB case demonstrates. Second, we evaluate whether
pathway specificity persists under frozen-weight transfer to
an independent dataset, addressing the concern that explana￾tion conclusions may be dataset-specific [8], [31]. The audit
protocol is thus an explanation evaluation method, not an
explanation generation method.
E. Methodological Implications
The protocol is model-agnostic by design. It can be
applied to any classifier that accepts 12-lead ECG input—we
demonstrated it across three raw-signal architectures (ResNet,
SE-ResNet, Transformer), with XGBoost baselines providing
complementary feature-space context. Applying the protocol
to different architectures revealed that pathway behavior can
vary across models even when trained on identical data:
the Transformer’s architecture-specific rhythm weakness and
XGBoost’s complementary AFIB feature use illustrate that
pathway evidence is not monolithic. A single-architecture
application of the protocol to ResNet would still produce
valid per-model conclusions (e.g., CLBBB pathway-supported,
1AVB not supported). The cross-architecture demonstration
confirms that the protocol does not tie its conclusions to a
specific model class.
Matched controls are not optional. The 1AVB case
demonstrates that large target-pathway effects can coexist with
even larger non-target dependence. Without matched controls,
1AVB would have been misclassified as a timing-specific
success. Every pathway claim in the audit protocol must
survive a matched-control specificity comparison, and the ASS
metric operationalizes this requirement directly.
External transfer separates stable from unstable path￾way claims. The protocol’s second key design element—
frozen-weight transfer to an independent, cardiologist￾validated dataset—acts as a stress test for pathway specificity.
CRBBB and CLBBB survive this test on all three architec￾tures under the primary operator (PTB-XL ASS positive with
CI> 0, CDDC= 1.0 for all 6 model-disease pairs). This is
the protocol’s central positive finding: QRS-morphology path￾way specificity is architecture-invariant and dataset-invariant.
1AVB external transfer confirms negative ASS on all three ar￾chitectures, corroborating the matched-control reversal. AFIB
external transfer reveals the zero-masking positive as operator
artifact—ASS is negative on both datasets under the primary
operator. The combination of external transfer and operator

without external transfer, SBRAD-ResNet’s internal positive

Interpretation boundaries. To clarify what the current
audit design can and cannot support, we distinguish four levels
of evidence:
1) Pathway sensitivity: Perturbation of the target region
causes a performance drop.
2) Pathway specificity: The target-region drop exceeds the
drop from matched control perturbations (ASS> 0).
3) Mechanistic validity: The model uses the same physi￾ological mechanisms that clinicians employ.
4) Clinical validity: The mechanism holds under physician
annotation or predicts real clinical outcomes.
The audit conclusions in this paper are structured around
pathway sensitivity and specificity (levels 1–2). Claims about
mechanistic or clinical validity (levels 3–4) require additional
evidence—clinician review of failure cases, formal mediation
analysis, or prospective validation—that is beyond the scope of
this study. This audit supports evidence plausibility under a
controlled perturbation protocol, not mechanistic causality
or clinical utility. Pathway-supported designations indicate
that a model’s predictions are more sensitive to disease￾relevant than to control-region perturbation under a primary
operator; they do not certify that the model uses the same
physiological mechanisms as a clinician, nor that the model is
safe for deployment.
Patient-level splitting, multi-seed training, and compre￾hensive metrics are essential protocol-level practices that
prevent data leakage, confirm training stability (within-split
SD= 0.0025), and capture the full performance picture beyond
a single metric. The representation ladder confirms that feature
complementarity operates across three axes (rhythm, morphol￾ogy, timing), and that explicit proxy features can recover
clinically relevant signal without end-to-end learning.

I. INTRODUCTION
Deep learning classifiers for electrocardiogram (ECG) anal￾ysis now achieve high discrimination across a growing set of
cardiac conditions [1]–[4], aided by large public datasets such
as PTB-XL [5] and CODE-15% [6]. But strong discrimination
does not tell us whether a model relies on disease-relevant
signal regions—a gap that matters for clinical deployment
beyond benchmark performance. A 1AVB classifier might
depend on QRS morphology instead of PR-interval timing; an
AFIB classifier might use ventricular rate irregularity, atrial
waveform features, or unrelated shortcuts. Standard bench￾mark metrics cannot distinguish these cases. Moreover, exist￾ing explanation methods rarely test whether disease-relevant
regions dominate over matched controls, or whether pathway
dependence holds up under dataset shift—sensitivity is not
specificity, and explanation conclusions can be fragile under
distribution shift [7], [8].
We address these gaps with a model-agnostic, matched￾control perturbation audit protocol. For each diagnosis we
pre-specify an expected positive pathway (e.g., the PR-target
window for 1AVB, the QRS complex for bundle branch block)
and compare targeted perturbations against anatomically adja￾cent control regions that should matter less. A pathway claim
is accepted only if the target perturbation is more disruptive
than its strongest matched control—a stricter criterion than
perturbation sensitivity alone. We further evaluate pathway
specificity under frozen-weight transfer from CODE-15% to

The protocol is model-agnostic: the same perturbation design
applies to any classifier accepting 12-lead ECG input, and
the five diseases are a case-study panel chosen to span three
diagnostic pathway categories (timing, morphology, rhythm),
not an exhaustive clinical survey.
We instantiate the matched-control waveform audit across
three raw-signal architectures (ResNet, SE-ResNet, and a
lightweight Transformer). Feature-space XGBoost baselines

The protocol is evaluated internally on CODE-15% (345,779

(cardiologist-validated labels).
Our primary contribution is the audit protocol itself—a
structured method for evaluating whether ECG classifiers base
decisions on disease-relevant signal regions, rather than on
correlated but clinically non-specific features. We show that
a matched-control design with external transfer can separate

(which requires evidence about how models arrive at deci￾sions).
II. RELATED WORK
A. ECG Classification with Deep Learning
1D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and residual
architectures have become the dominant paradigm for auto￾mated ECG classification. Hannun et al. [1] demonstrated
cardiologist-level arrhythmia detection using a 34-layer 1D
CNN on ambulatory ECGs. On the PTB-XL benchmark,
Strodthoff et al. [2] established strong baselines with 1D
ResNets and fully convolutional networks across 71 diagnostic
classes; their follow-up review [3] confirmed that ResNet-style
architectures remain competitive against newer alternatives.
Mehari and Strodthoff [9] further advanced PTB-XL bench￾marks through self-supervised pre-training, while Chen et
al. [10] and Zubair et al. [11] contributed targeted architectures
for multi-class and imbalanced ECG classification.
Beyond vanilla ResNets, SE-ResNet [12] adds channel-wise
attention, and lightweight Transformer adaptations [13] have
been applied via patch-based self-attention. Recent hybrid
architectures combine these paradigms—Cardioformer [14]
couples multi-granularity patching with Transformer layers,
while xECGArch [15] separates morphology and rhythm pro￾cessing with dual CNNs. ECG-JEPA [16] pushed PTB-XL
performance to AUROC=0.945 through JEPA pre-training
on over one million records spanning ten datasets including
CODE-15%. Foundation models such as ECG-FM [17] fur￾ther scale pre-training, though their explanation behavior and
pathway-level auditability remain unexplored. Prior to the deep
learning era, classical machine learning methods—including
XGBoost, random forests, and support vector machines—
were widely applied to handcrafted ECG features and remain
competitive baselines on structured feature sets [18], [19].
Despite these advances across both classical and deep
learning paradigms, the common evaluation framework em￾phasizes discrimination metrics on held-out test splits. It
remains unclear whether these models base their decisions
on disease-relevant signal regions, and whether region-specific
dependence survives cross-dataset transfer. This gap motivates
our multi-level audit protocol, which applies identical pathway
questions across representation levels—from a feature-based
XGBoost baseline to a raw-signal ResNet—allowing us to
assess pathway dependence across both classical and deep
learning models.
B. Explainability and Perturbation Methods
Post-hoc explanation methods—including saliency maps,
occlusion-based sensitivity, guided backpropagation, and in￾tegrated gradients—have been systematically evaluated on
ECG tasks. Storas et al. [20] compared nine gradient-based ˚
methods on synthetic 12-lead ECGs and found that no single
method works best across all measurement tasks, with con￾siderable disagreement between human expert evaluation and
perturbation-based metrics. Suh et al. [21] evaluated eleven
attribution methods across five large ECG datasets and re￾ported that Guided Grad-CAM best aligned with cardiologists’
assessment while localization-based metrics better reflected
human judgment than perturbation-based ones. Plagwitz et
al. [22] assessed the reliability of feature attribution explana￾tions in ECG analysis through systematic perturbation testing,
reporting that explanation reliability varies substantially across
attribution methods and disease categories. Al-Zaiti et al. [23]
found that clinically deployed saliency maps for occlusion
MI detection were rated only slightly clinically relevant by
practicing clinicians, underscoring the gap between current
explanation quality and clinical expectations.
Perturbation-based evaluation—in which input regions are
removed or altered to measure prediction change—provides
a more direct test of feature dependence than gradient-based
attributions alone. Wagner et al. [24] proposed a structured
XAI framework for ECG that combines occlusion-based san￾ity checks, glocal attribution aggregation, and concept-based
analysis, providing quantitative evidence that model behav￾ior can align with cardiologists’ decision rules. Bender et
al. [25] demonstrated that a ResNet trained for 12-lead ECG
classification learns features analogous to clinical diagnostic
criteria including P-wave morphology, QRS duration, and
PR interval. Recent work has also applied wave masking

their approach requires ground-truth explanation annotations

Despite these advances, three structural limitations persist
across the existing ECG explanation literature. First, existing
perturbation studies rarely incorporate matched anatomical
controls: they test whether a region matters, but not whether
disease-specific regions matter more than adjacent control
regions. This is the key distinction between perturbation
sensitivity (a region is important) and anatomical specificity (a
disease-specific region is more important than its anatomically
adjacent controls)—a distinction we operationalize through the
ASS metric and matched-control design. Second, explanation
conclusions are typically validated only within the training
distribution. Adebayo et al. [7] showed that saliency maps
can fail basic sanity checks under simple input transfor￾mations, Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola [30] demonstrated that
interpretability methods can be fragile under input pertur￾bations, and Ong Ly et al. [31] demonstrated that hidden

performance by up to 20%, with AUROC dropping from 0.90

broadly, DeGrave et al. [32] showed that deep learning models
for radiographic COVID-19 detection selected clinically irrele￾vant shortcuts over meaningful signal—a finding that directly
parallels our concern about ECG classifiers exploiting non￾specific waveform features. Third, few studies test whether
explanation claims survive external dataset shift [8]. These
gaps directly motivate our matched-control perturbation design
with frozen-weight cross-dataset transfer.
C. Dataset Use and Cross-Dataset Validation
The two largest public 12-lead ECG datasets—PTB-XL [5]
(21,837 records, cardiologist-validated labels) and CODE-15%
[6] (345,779 exams, automated labels)—have enabled a wide
range of deep learning studies. PTB-XL provides carefully
annotated multi-label diagnoses with rich metadata including
signal quality indicators and demographic attributes, while
CODE-15% offers an order of magnitude more samples but
with labels derived from an automated interpretation system.
This label-source asymmetry introduces a critical distinction:
models trained on CODE-15% may learn to replicate the
automated labeling logic rather than physician-level diagnostic
features, creating a label circularity risk that varies by disease
category. The PTB-XL+ dataset [33] supplements PTB-XL
with 71 handcrafted features spanning heart rate variability,
QRS morphology, and signal quality metrics, enabling direct
comparisons between learned representations and classical
ECG parameters.
Cross-dataset validation remains underutilized in the ECG
deep learning literature, and where it has been attempted,
the results are sobering. Bickmann et al. [18] benchmarked
time-series versus feature-based methods on PTB-XL but
did not include external validation. Soltanieh et al. [34]
addressed out-of-distribution generalization for self-supervised
ECG representations, showing that dataset shift degrades stan￾dard supervised baselines. Frank et al. [35] reported that
models achieving AUROC>0.90 within-dataset for myocardial
ischemia detection experienced substantial performance drops
across six public ECG databases. At the foundation-model
scale, ECGFounder [36] and recent benchmarking efforts [37]
confirm that cross-domain generalization remains a key chal￾lenge even for large pre-trained models with diverse training
data.
The consistent picture is that external validation across
datasets with different label sources, populations, and acqui￾sition protocols is widely recommended but rarely executed,
and even less often applied to explanation claims. Our study
addresses this gap through frozen-weight transfer from CODE￾15% to cardiologist-validated PTB-XL fold 10, treating the
external dataset as a simultaneous check on both prediction
quality and pathway explanation consistency.
D. Clinical Pathway and Mechanistic Analysis
Clinical ECG interpretation relies on well-defined phys￾iological features: PR interval for atrioventricular conduc￾tion timing, QRS duration and morphology for ventricular
conduction, RR interval regularity for rhythm classification,
and P-wave morphology for atrial activity assessment [38].
These features define distinct diagnostic pathways for condi￾tions such as 1AVB (prolonged PR>200ms), bundle branch
blocks (wide QRS>120ms with characteristic terminal/lateral
R patterns), sinus bradycardia (low ventricular rate), and atrial
fibrillation (absent or fibrillatory atrial activity).
Recent studies have directly tested whether deep ECG
models learn these clinically meaningful features. Hempel et
al. [39] extended an XAI framework to match deep learning
relevances with PR interval and QRS duration from PTB-XL+,
reporting that 96.0% of high-confidence 1AVB predictions had
PR>200ms and 98.6% of high-confidence LBBB predictions
had QRS>120ms—strong evidence that the model internally
represents clinical thresholds. Riberg et al. [40] performed a
concordance analysis between ResNet predictions and cardi￾ology guideline thresholds, finding that RR interval features
dominated for sinus bradycardia and tachycardia while mor￾phological features showed weaker correlation. Hammer et
al. [41] introduced an architecture that explicitly separates
rhythm (long-term) and morphology (short-term) processing,
demonstrating that fused explanations correlate with clinical
diagnostic criteria. A systematic review by Ayano et al. [42]
confirmed that interpretable ML studies for ECG increasingly
target clinical parameters such as PR interval, QRS duration,
and RR variability.
Despite this progress, a critical gap remains: existing studies
confirm that models attend to clinically relevant features,
but they do not test whether a disease-specific signal region
dominates over anatomically adjacent controls, or whether
such pathway specificity survives dataset shift. Demonstrating
feature relevance is not the same as demonstrating feature

audit addresses this gap: for five diagnoses spanning timing,

III. METHODS
A. Study Overview: Matched-Control Pathway Audit
Standard discrimination metrics (AUROC, F1) cannot dis￾tinguish a model that uses disease-relevant signal regions from
one that exploits statistically correlated but mechanistically ir￾relevant shortcuts. Our audit protocol is designed to make this
distinction explicit. Fig. 1 summarizes the overall workflow,
which proceeds in four stages:
1) Disease-centered audit panel: For each of five diag￾noses spanning timing (1AVB), morphology (CRBBB,
CLBBB), and rhythm (SBRAD, AFIB) pathways, we
pre-specify an expected positive pathway grounded in
clinical ECG diagnostic criteria, together with anatomi￾cally matched control regions (Section III-C).
2) Matched-control perturbation: The same perturbation
operator is applied to both the target region and each
matched control. A pathway claim requires the target
perturbation to be more disruptive than its strongest
matched control—not merely that it produces a large
effect. Perturbations fall into two classes depending on
whether the diagnostic feature is temporally localized or
globally distributed (Section III-D).
3) Audit metrics and evidence tiers: A matched-control
comparison metric quantifies anatomical specificity. Per￾model evidence tiers classify each (architecture, disease)
pair under a predefined primary operator, constraining
what can be claimed from the observed perturbation
patterns (Section III-E).
4) External validation: Frozen-weight transfer from
CODE-15% to cardiologist-validated PTB-XL fold 10
checks whether pathway conclusions survive dataset
shift (Section III-B).
The protocol is model-agnostic: the same perturbation
windows, matched-control comparisons, and evaluation met￾rics apply to any classifier accepting 12-lead ECG input.
We demonstrate this across three raw-signal architectures,
with XGBoost feature-space baselines providing contextual
representation-level evidence (Section III-F). The five diag￾noses are a case-study panel spanning three diagnostic path￾way categories, not an exhaustive clinical survey.
B. Datasets and External Validation Setting
Internal cohort — CODE-15%. Brazilian 12-lead ECG
dataset: 345,779 exams (400Hz, 10 s) from 233,770 patients
[6]. Labels were derived from an automated ECG interpreta￾tion system. This dataset serves as the training and internal
audit cohort: all models are trained on CODE-15%, and all
internal perturbation audit experiments are conducted on its
held-out test set. Patient-level split: 60% train (207,232), 20%
validation (69,045), 20% test (69,520), random seed 42.
Label circularity risk. Because CODE-15% labels are au￾tomated rather than physician-adjudicated, models trained
on them may learn to replicate the automated labeling
logic instead of physician-level diagnostic mechanisms. The
risk varies: 1AVB (highest, PR>200 ms threshold overlap),
SBRAD (high, HR-based rules), CRBBB/CLBBB (moderate,
QRS morphology criteria), AFIB (moderate, atrial activity
metrics). Internal CODE findings should therefore be in￾terpreted as evidence about model behavior relative to the
automated-label system, not as physician-equivalent diagnostic
reasoning. External validation on cardiologist-validated labels
(below) provides the primary credibility buffer.
External cohort — PTB-XL. German 12-lead ECG
dataset: 21,837 records from 18,885 patients at 500 Hz [5].
We use the official patient-level folds: folds 1–8 for reference,
fold 9 (n = 2, 183) for threshold retuning, and fold 10
(n = 2, 198) for testing. Fold 10 labels were validated by
cardiologists and serve as the primary external credibility set—
the key check against CODE-15% label circularity. SCP-ECG
diagnostic codes were mapped to the five target diseases using
strict primary code matching.
Transfer and evaluation protocol. CODE-trained models
are applied to PTB-XL without fine-tuning (frozen weights).
PTB-XL signals are downsampled from 500 Hz to 400 Hz via
Fourier resampling, trimmed/padded to 4,096 samples, and z￾score normalized per lead with lead order matching CODE￾15%. We report three transfer levels to bound performance:
(1) strict frozen—CODE validation thresholds applied directly
to fold 10; (2) calibrated—thresholds retuned on fold 9; (3)
oracle upper bound—optimal thresholds on fold 10. AU￾ROC is threshold-invariant and serves as the primary frozen￾generalization metric; F1 depends on operating-point choice.
C. Disease-Centered Audit Panel
The audit framework is built around a compact, literature￾guided panel covering five diagnoses. For each disease we
pre-specify (i) the expected positive pathway, (ii) matched
control regions that should produce smaller effects, and (iii)
any ambiguous pathway treated as hypothesis-testing.
Clinical anchoring. Each target region and control pairing
is grounded in established ECG diagnostic criteria [38]. The
target maps to the clinically accepted diagnostic feature for
that disease (PR prolongation for 1AVB, QRS widening for
BBB, low ventricular rate for SBRAD, absent P-waves for
AFIB). Each matched control is anatomically adjacent but
physiologically distinct (e.g., ST segment vs PR-target per￾turbation window, QRS complex vs atrial window), so that an
informative control comparison is possible: the control probes
a plausible alternative signal channel rather than a trivially
irrelevant region.

primary operator.

G. Statistical Analysis
Uncertainty quantification: Patient-level bootstrap confi￾dence intervals (1,000 replicates, seed 42) are the primary
uncertainty quantification throughout this paper [43]. For
the perturbation audit, bootstrap replicates resample patients
(not individual ECGs) with replacement; all ECGs belonging
to a resampled patient are included, preserving the within￾patient correlation structure. ASS is computed on the paired
target-versus-control perturbation effects within each replicate,
maintaining the matched-subject design.
Model comparison: Pairwise model comparisons (ResNet
vs XGBoost Simple, ResNet vs XGBoost Clinical-MVP, XG￾Boost Clinical-MVP vs Simple) were performed per disease
on the shared test set. For AUROC, we used the DeLong
test [44] for paired comparisons on identical test samples.
For F1, we used vectorized paired permutation tests with
5,000 resamples [45]. Two-sided p-values were computed as
the proportion of |permuted ∆F1| ≥ |observed ∆F1|. Holm￾Bonferroni correction was applied to the family of 18 compar￾isons (3 model pairs × 5 diseases + 3 macro-F1). We note that
permutation p-values and DeLong tests operate at the sample
level (n ≈ 69, 500 ECGs from approximately 47,000 unique
patients; mean 1.48 samples/patient); because within-patient
correlations reduce the effective sample size, sample-level tests
may produce optimistic p-values and are reported for com￾pleteness as approximate secondary indicators. Patient-level
bootstrap CIs provide the primary uncertainty quantification.
Multiplicity control for external pathway tests: The
primary external audit tests 15 pre-specified hypotheses of
the form H0 : ASS ≤ 0 (one-sided) under the primary
linear-interpolation operator on PTB-XL fold 10. We apply
the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) pro￾cedure at α = 0.05 to control the expected proportion of false
positives among rejected hypotheses. Bootstrap p-values are
computed as 1−Pr(ASS¿0), where Pr(ASS> 0) is the fraction
of bootstrap replicates with positive ASS. Storey q-values are
reported alongside BH-FDR thresholds (Table XIII).
Cross-dataset feature-space validation: XGBoost models
were also trained on PTB-XL+ 12SL features (783D) using
official PTB-XL patient-level folds (1–8 train, 9 validation
for threshold tuning, 10 test) [18], [33]. Labels were mapped
from SCP-ECG codes to the 5 target diseases using strict
primary diagnostic codes only. For 1AVB contextualization,
a PR>200ms rule baseline was computed using NeuroKit2’s
wavelet-based ECG delineation on the original 500Hz signal;
the continuous PR interval AUROC is compared against
ResNet AUROC via the DeLong test.
IV. RESULTS
A. Baseline Discrimination Establishes the Context for Path￾way Auditing
We first establish the discrimination context for the
matched-control audit. This step is methodological rather than
a primary result: the audit asks whether a functioning classifier
uses disease-consistent signal pathways, and a negative audit
result is interpretable only if the model has learned the disease
label to a nontrivial degree. Otherwise, ASS ≤ 0 could reflect
either absent pathway specificity or classification failure.
The audited raw-signal models generally achieved strong
discrimination on the five-disease panel. ResNet reached AU￾ROC > 0.98 for all five diseases (Table IV), with Micro￾F1= 0.736, and SE-ResNet was statistically indistinguishable
from ResNet. The lightweight Transformer preserved BBB
detection (CRBBB F1 0.805; CLBBB 0.807) but was weaker
on rhythm disorders (SBRAD F1 0.284; AFIB F1 0.585), a
limitation considered when interpreting its rhythm-pathway

be treated as a secondary implementation detail. A single￾operator study using zero-masking would have concluded

feature-space context, it reveals that pathway-specific evidence
is not uniform across models—even when discrimination met￾rics are uniformly high. We present findings per architecture to
show what the protocol reveals for each model independently.

perturbation effect is reversed by matched QRS controls,

both datasets—supporting the protocol’s core argument that
target-only perturbation is insufficient for pathway claims.

B. Why Discrimination Metrics Alone Are Insufficient
A central claim of this paper is that standard discrimination
metrics—F1, AUROC, AUPRC—are necessary but insufficient
for evaluating whether a classifier uses disease-consistent
signal pathways under this audit. The audit results provide
specific evidence for this claim.
All five diseases achieve AUROC> 0.98 on ResNet. Yet the
per-model audit reveals categories invisible to discrimination
metrics alone: (i) Not supported—1AVB on all three architec￾tures (matched controls reverse the conclusion); AFIB on all
three architectures (atrial-window ASS negative under primary
operator on both datasets); SBRAD on SE-ResNet and Trans￾former (rate-pathway ASS negative). (ii) Evidence-limited—
SBRAD on ResNet only (rate-pathway positive internally
and externally, but external CI crosses zero). (iii) Pathway￾supported—CRBBB and CLBBB on all three architectures
(positive ASS with external replication under primary operator
on both datasets). All five diseases would be classified as
“successful” under a discrimination-only evaluation, but the
per-model audit reveals that 6 of 15 model-disease pairs
reach Pathway-supported, 1 is Evidence-limited, and 8 are Not
supported.
Conversely, a model need not achieve the highest dis￾crimination to provide trustworthy pathway behavior. The
Transformer underperforms ResNet on discrimination (Micro￾F1 0.6045 vs 0.7359) but preserves BBB detection with near￾identical F1—and its architecture-specific rhythm weakness is
informative. The protocol thus evaluates models along an axis
orthogonal to discrimination: a model can be accurate without
using pathway-specific signal, and a model can be less accurate
while still providing informative pathway signals.

The audit protocol also serves as a critique of explanation
evaluation practices that rely on single-region perturbation or
attribution without matched controls. The 1AVB case provides
the clearest demonstration.
A standard perturbation study would test whether perturbing
the PR-target window degrades 1AVB detection. The effect is
large (∆AUROC= −0.226), clinically plausible (the PR in￾terval defines 1AVB), and robust across perturbation methods
(zero-masking, inpainting, Gaussian noise). A conventional ex￾plainability study would stop here and conclude that the model
depends specifically on PR-window information—a publish￾able positive result. But our protocol requires one additional
comparison: matched QRS perturbation. On the same matched
cohort, QRS perturbation is even more disruptive, yielding
negative ASS on both CODE and PTB-XL under all three
tested operators. The operator-comparison battery confirms
this across two architectures: ResNet 1AVB ASS≤ −0.010

These may contain embedded text in images, infographics, complex tables, diagrams, and other visual elements not fully captured in the parsed text.
You can directly view these images to read text within images, interpret infographics, understand diagrams and complex tables. When applicable, combine insights from both parsed text and images to provide comprehensive and enriched answers.

When responding to the user, actively incorporate information from embedded text, images, tables, diagrams, and other visuals in the files when applicable.
Explicitly reference them by mentioning their location (e.g., page number) and summarizing their content. For example:
- "According to the *chart on page 5*, sales have increased by 20% over ..."
- "The *diagram on page 3* illustrates the workflow, highlighting ..."

The file contents provided above are truncated/partial snippets. The complete content for these files IS accessible via querying.

If the user asks a question related to these files, and the provided snippets do not clearly answer it, you **MUST** use the `file_search` tool to search the full document contents before responding.

## How to invoke the file_search tool
If the user's query isn't sufficiently answered by the provided snippets, parsed text, or images, you should invoke `file_search.msearch`.
To search the full content of the available files, you **must** send one message with recipient `to=file_search.msearch` in the analysis channel. Your message should be structured exactly as follows:
```
{
  'queries': ['Example query 1', 'Example query 2']  // List of up to five queries to search for.
}
```

Carefully balance the number of `file_search` calls and the quality of your response with the latency incurred by `file_search` calls.

Important guidelines for query formatting:
- Your message must be a valid JSON object. Do not include any extraneous text, backticks, markdown formatting, or comments beyond what is shown.
- The `queries` field must be a list of strings.
- One of the queries **MUST** exactly match the user's original question, but stripped of any extraneous details, and with ambiguous references clearly resolved using context from the conversation. It **MUST** be a complete sentence.
- Even if you suspect the user meant something else, one query **MUST** still be their original question.

## How to handle results from file_search
The file search tool will respond with the relevant search results from the full files. After you receive these results:
- Carefully evaluate each result to determine its relevance and quality.
- Use the high-quality and relevant results to inform your answer to the user's question.
- When possible, reuse information from prior file_search results and avoid repeating identical queries.

## Tool usage instructions and ordering
When the user asks a question, carefully consider whether the provided snippets sufficiently answer the query, whether you need to invoke `file_search.msearch`, or another available tool (such as `web`, if available) should be used instead.

Tool-ordering Guidelines:
1. For queries related to uploaded files, if snippets are insufficient, strongly prefer invoking `file_search.msearch` over other tools.
    - Avoid using `web.run`, `python` analysis, or any other tools until you have either:
        - Confirmed with high confidence the answer is not in the files, or
        - Have high confidence `file_search_tool` queries are not sufficient to answer the query.
2. Avoid usage of `web_search/web.run` for queries related to uploaded files
    - Carefully consider whether the user's query is better answered by web search results rather than available snippets or results from `file_search_tool`.
    - Unless the user's query is clearly unrelated to the uploaded files, prefer using `file_search.msearch`. You can always follow up with a web search if necessary for a more complete response.
3. Avoid using `python` unless necessary or requested by user.
    - If the user's query is answerable from the parsed text and images from the uploaded files, or from `file_search_tool`, do not invoke `python`.

Always keep this instruction in mind for the rest of the conversation, as the user may reference these files or ask related questions later on.

perturbation effect is reversed by matched QRS controls,
yielding negative ASS under all tested operators and on
both datasets—supporting the protocol’s core argument that
target-only perturbation is insufficient for pathway claims.

parts:
我赞成你老师的判断：**Results 不应该再按“模型性能 → 一堆实验结果”线性展开，而应该按“审计方法能回答什么问题”来组织。**  
你现在的定位清楚后，Results 的核心不是“我们模型分类好不好”，而是：

> 给定一个能分类的模型，审计方法能否判断它是否真正使用了预期医学通路；这种判断是否经得起 matched controls、架构变化、外部数据迁移和统计检验。

所以基础性能不应作为一个完整 Results 小节保留。它可以保留，但要**降级为审计前提/有效性检查**。

---

## 1. 我建议删掉现在的 “A. Baseline Discrimination...” 独立小节

你现在 A 小节的问题是：它虽然写得比以前清楚了，但它还是把读者带回了“分类性能论文”的语境。

现在 A 的核心逻辑是对的：

> 只有模型本身能分类，ASS 的负结果才有解释意义；否则负 ASS 可能只是模型坏了。

但这不是一个主要发现，而是一个 **eligibility check / audit prerequisite**。

所以建议改成 Results 开头的一个短段落，最多 1 个小表或一句引用表格，不要单独编号成主小节。

可以写成类似：

> Before applying the pathway audit, we verified that each audited raw-signal model achieved non-trivial discrimination on the five-disease panel. This check is not a primary result, but an interpretability prerequisite: a negative ASS is meaningful only when the classifier can recognize the disease label. All audited raw-signal models satisfied this requirement; therefore, the following results evaluate pathway use rather than classification failure.

然后把详细 F1/AUROC 表移到 Supplement，主文只保留：

- ResNet / SE-ResNet 性能足够；
- Transformer 在 rhythm 任务较弱，因此 rhythm audit 解释要谨慎；
- XGBoost 只是 feature-space context，不进入 waveform audit tier。

这就够了。

---

## 2. Results 的主线应该改成“四个审计问题”

你现在的 CDEF 其实已经接近正确结构，但仍有一点散：有些地方像 case study，有些地方像 architecture comparison，有些地方像 external validation，有些地方又回到 operator artifact。建议明确改成四个审计问题。

我建议 Results 结构如下：

---

# IV. Results

## A. Audited Models Are Sufficiently Discriminative for Pathway Audit  
**短小节，或直接作为 Results 开头段落。**

目的不是展示性能，而是声明：

> 后续 ASS 结果不是因为模型不会分类。

不要在这里展开性能比较。Table IV/V 可以压缩或放补充材料。

---

## B. Matched Controls Prevent False Pathway Claims

这是你论文最重要的方法论结果。  
建议把 **1AVB** 放在这里作为 anchor case。

这一节的中心句应该是：

> Target-only perturbation would have falsely suggested PR-pathway use for 1AVB, but matched QRS controls reversed the conclusion.

这节不要混太多其他病种。重点讲清楚：

1. PR occlusion 确实造成大 drop；
2. 如果只看 target perturbation，会得出“模型使用 PR 通路”的结论；
3. matched QRS control 更大；
4. 因此 ASS < 0；
5. 外部 PTB-XL 也重复这个 reversal；
6. 结论：**sensitivity is not specificity**。

这一节最好只服务一个目的：证明 matched-control audit 的必要性。

你现在 1AVB 写得比较长，有些细节如 PR-window overlap sensitivity 可以放 Supplement 或 Discussion 轻提。主文不宜展开太多，否则会把 B 小节拖成方法补充。

---

## C. The Same Audit Reveals Model-Specific, Not Disease-Intrinsic, Pathway Use

这是你现在 “Model-Level Pathway Evidence Under a Shared Audit Protocol” 的核心，但标题可以更锋利。

这一节回答的问题是：

> 同一个疾病、同一个医学通路，不同模型是否都会使用？

这里应按结果类型组织，而不是逐个实验流水账。

建议分三类：

### C1. Robust pathway use: BBB / QRS morphology  
CRBBB 和 CLBBB 是你的强阳性结果。  
要突出：

- 三个架构都 ASS > 0；
- 内部和外部一致；
- 说明 QRS morphology 是模型稳定使用的医学通路；
- 这是审计方法的 positive control / successful pathway-supported case。

### C2. Matched-control failure: 1AVB / PR prolongation  
这里可以简短引用 B 的发现，不要重复太多。  
强调：

- PR perturbation 有效；
- 但不是 pathway-specific；
- all models Not supported。

### C3. Architecture-dependent pathway use: SBRAD / rate  
这是你的“审计不是给疾病贴标签，而是审计具体模型”的关键证据。

重点写：

- ResNet 内部 positive，外部方向一致但 CI 跨零，所以 Evidence-limited；
- SE-ResNet 和 Transformer 不支持；
- 因此“低心率通路”不是所有模型自然都会学到；
- 这正好支持你新定位：**audit individual models, not disease labels**。

### C4. Negative / artifact-prone pathway claim: AFIB atrial activity  
AFIB 要小心写，因为它很容易让读者问：“那 AFIB 模型到底用了什么？”  
你不需要在 Results 中完整回答它用了什么，而是说：

- atrial-window pathway under primary operator 不支持；
- RR irregularity audit 也没有形成支持性机制；
- zero-masking 的阳性被 primary operator 推翻；
- 这是 operator artifact 的警示案例。

这一节不要写成“AFIB 失败了”，而要写成：

> The audit rejected a plausible but unsupported pathway claim.

这个很符合你的方法论文定位。

---

## D. External Transfer Tests Whether Audited Pathway Use Survives Dataset Shift

这一节要和你现在的 “External Transfer as an Audit Stress Test” 对齐，但建议减少普通 transfer performance 的篇幅。

你的新定位里，外部迁移不是为了证明模型泛化多强，而是为了证明：

> 在设备、采集习惯、人群、标签来源变化时，医学通路是否仍是模型决策依据。

所以 D 的主句应该是：

> External validation is used not merely to report transfer performance, but to stress-test whether pathway-specific evidence persists under dataset shift.

这一节建议保留：

- PTB-XL fold 10 cardiologist-validated；
- frozen-weight inference；
- AUROC 足够，说明模型可用；
- 关键是 external ASS；
- BBB 保持 Pathway-supported；
- 1AVB/AFIB 保持 Not supported；
- SBRAD-ResNet Evidence-limited；
- SE-ResNet SBRAD 出现 sign reversal，说明 pathway evidence can be dataset/model dependent。

这里不建议把 threshold retuning、oracle F1、PR>200ms rule baseline 写太长。它们可以压到 Supplement 或作为一句 “operating-point context”。

---

## E. Evidence-Tier Summary: What the Audit Concludes for Each Model-Pathway Pair

这一节应该成为 Results 的“收束表”。

也就是你现在 Table XI + forest plot 的位置。

这里不要再重复每个 disease 的完整解释。应该用一张表和一段总结完成：

- 6 个 Pathway-supported：CRBBB / CLBBB × 3 architectures；
- 1 个 Evidence-limited：SBRAD-ResNet；
- 其余 Not supported：1AVB、AFIB、SBRAD on SE-ResNet/Transformer；
- 结论：高分类性能不等于 pathway-consistent reasoning；
- 审计结果是 model-specific。

这节可以非常有力，因为它直接回应你论文标题 “Beyond Discrimination”。

---

## F. Confirmatory Inference Supports the Tier Assignments

这一节可以保留，但要更短。  
它不是一个新的故事，而是对 E 的统计确认。

建议写成：

> Multiplicity-controlled inference did not change any tier assignment.

然后讲：

- 6 个 BBB pathway-supported pairs survive FDR；
- SBRAD-ResNet 不过 FDR，因此维持 Evidence-limited；
- SE-ResNet SBRAD 外部阳性但内部阴性，所以仍 Not supported；
- no tier changes。

这一节不宜太长，否则 Results 结尾会显得技术性过重。

---

## 3. 你现在 Results 最大的问题：重复叙事太多

目前同一个结论在多个地方反复出现：

- 1AVB negative ASS 在 B、C、E、Discussion 都讲；
- BBB positive ASS 在 C、D、E 都讲；
- AFIB zero-masking artifact 在 B、C、E 都讲；
- SBRAD Evidence-limited 在 C、D、E、F 都讲。

修改时要给每一节分工：

| 小节 | 只回答这个问题 | 不要做的事 |
|---|---|---|
| A / opening | 模型是否具备审计资格？ | 不展开性能论文式比较 |
| B | 为什么 matched controls 必要？ | 不全面总结所有疾病 |
| C | 审计在不同架构上发现什么？ | 不重复外部迁移细节 |
| D | pathway evidence 是否跨数据集保持？ | 不写太多普通 F1/AUROC |
| E | 最终 tier 是什么？ | 不再讲完整 case story |
| F | 统计检验是否改变结论？ | 不重新解释医学意义 |

这样文章会紧很多。

---

## 4. 我会建议 Results 主标题这样改

你现在的标题偏“实验项目罗列”。可以改成更有方法论文气质的标题：

### 原 A  
**Baseline Discrimination Establishes the Context for Pathway Auditing**

建议改为：

**Audit Eligibility: Models Achieve Sufficient Discrimination**

甚至不设小节，放 Results 开头。

---

### 原 B  
**The Case for Matched Controls: 1AVB as Anchor Demonstration**

这个标题不错，但可以更锋利：

**Matched Controls Reverse a Target-Only 1AVB Pathway Claim**

这个标题一看就知道你的贡献是什么。

---

### 原 C  
**Model-Level Pathway Evidence Under a Shared Audit Protocol**

建议改为：

**Pathway Evidence Is Model-Specific Under a Shared Audit Protocol**

更贴合你的新定位。

---

### 原 D  
**External Transfer as an Audit Stress Test**

这个标题很好，可以保留。  
也可以稍微加强：

**External Transfer Stress-Tests Whether Pathway Evidence Survives Dataset Shift**

---

### 原 E  
**Case-Study Audit Summary**

建议改为：

**Evidence-Tier Summary Across Model–Pathway Pairs**

“Case-study” 会让人觉得你只是在讲案例，不像系统方法。

---

### 原 F  
**Confirmatory Inference: Clustered Bootstrap and Multiplicity Control**

可以保留，但建议更结果导向：

**Multiplicity-Controlled Inference Preserves the Audit Conclusions**

---

## 5. 基础性能到底保留多少？

我的建议很明确：

**保留，但不要作为主要 Results。**

原因是它在逻辑上必要，但在论文定位上不是贡献。

你可以这样处理：

### 主文保留
一小段 + 一个简化表/引用补充表：

- raw-signal models achieve sufficient AUROC/F1；
- Transformer rhythm performance weaker；
- XGBoost only feature-space context；
- therefore downstream audit interprets pathway use, not classifier failure。

### Supplement 放
- full per-disease performance；
- feature ablation；
- score distributions；
- XGBoost detailed results；
- multi-seed stability；
- paired permutation tests。

### 主文里不要再强调
- “ResNet AUROC > 0.98 for all diseases” 这种句子可以保留一句；
- 但不要让 Table IV、Table V 成为 Results 前两页的视觉中心。

因为读者一进 Results 看到两个性能表，会默认你是一个 classification paper。你现在不想让他们这样读。

---

## 6. 一个更紧的 Results 逻辑流

你可以把 Results 开头改成这种叙事：

> We report results according to the audit question rather than classifier performance. First, we verify that the audited models are sufficiently discriminative for ASS to be interpretable. We then show that matched controls are necessary by a 1AVB case in which target-only perturbation would give a false positive pathway claim. Next, we apply the same audit across architectures to test whether pathway evidence is model-specific. Finally, we use PTB-XL frozen transfer and multiplicity-controlled inference to determine which model–pathway claims remain supported under dataset shift and statistical correction.

这段放在 Results 开头，读者就不会迷路。

---

## 7. 我对 CDEF 是否保留的判断

你老师说“主要保留后四小节 CDEF”，我理解是对的，但我会稍微调整：

不是简单保留 CDEF，而是把 Results 改成：

1. **审计资格检查**：极短；
2. **matched controls 的必要性**：1AVB anchor；
3. **共享审计协议下的模型差异**：architecture-level；
4. **外部迁移压力测试**：dataset shift；
5. **最终 evidence tiers**：Table XI / forest plot；
6. **统计确认**：FDR / bootstrap。

也就是说，**你不是删除基础性能，而是把基础性能降级；不是保留 CDEF 原样，而是让它们围绕 audit claim 重新分工。**

---

## 8. 最关键的一句话

你这篇 Results 应该让读者记住的不是：

> 我们的模型 AUROC 很高。

而是：

> Even when discrimination is high, pathway use differs across models; matched-control auditing can distinguish true pathway-specific evidence from target sensitivity, operator artifacts, and dataset-dependent shortcuts.

围绕这句话改，Results 会紧很多，也会更像一篇“审计方法”论文。

A dedicated cardiologist-adjudicated
subset of CODE-15% remains important for formal label￾noise quantification. Lead-stratified perturbation experiments
with clinician review of failure cases would add anatomical
granularity beyond the current all-lead protocol. Extending
the audit panel to more diagnoses, incorporating subgroup
and fairness analyses, and evaluating hybrid models that
combine handcrafted features with learned representations
are natural next steps. More realistic perturbation designs—
including physiologically motivated simulations instead of
signal removal—could strengthen mechanistic interpretation.
Finally, the operator-comparison battery findings demonstrate
that perturbation operator choice is an important influence
on pathway conclusions in matched-control audit design; the
broader perturbation literature would benefit from community
standards on operator selection, preregistration, and mini￾mal reporting requirements for perturbation-based explanation
studies.
VI. CONCLUSION
We propose a model-agnostic matched-control pathway au￾dit protocol for evaluating pathway-specific evidence in ECG
classifiers. The protocol requires that (i) targeted perturba￾tions are compared against anatomically matched controls,
(ii) the perturbation operator is documented and compared
via a preregistered operator-comparison battery, (iii) path￾way specificity is re-tested under frozen-weight transfer to
an independent cardiologist-validated dataset, and (iv) per￾model evidence tiers—pathway-supported, evidence-limited,
not supported—are assigned to each (architecture, disease)
pair, constraining interpretation under operator dependence
and external transfer without aggregating across architectures.
Applied to five diagnoses as a case-study panel, the protocol
reveals heterogeneity invisible to discrimination metrics alone:
1AVB is Not supported across all three architectures on
both datasets—a replicated matched-control failure demon￾strating that target-only perturbation can produce false-positive
pathway claims; CRBBB and CLBBB both reach Pathway￾supported on all three architectures (internal+external positive
ASS with CI> 0 on both datasets, CDDC= 1.0 for all
6 pairs), confirming that QRS-morphology pathway speci￾ficity is architecture-invariant and dataset-invariant; SBRAD
splits—ResNet Evidence-limited (rate-pathway positive inter￾nally and externally but external CI narrowly crosses zero),
SE-ResNet and Transformer Not supported—demonstrating
that rate-pathway learning is architecture-dependent; AFIB is
Not supported on all three architectures on both datasets, with
its earlier zero-masking positive revealed as operator artifact.
Overall, 6 of 15 model-disease pairs reach Pathway-supported,
1 is Evidence-limited, and 8 are Not supported. The sole
Evidence-limited designation (SBRAD-ResNet) reflects nar￾row CI margin, not absent external data or protocol failure. A
preregistered operator-comparison battery shows that operator
choice strongly influences pathway conclusions: zero-masking
creates boundary artifacts that can reverse specificity, while
linear interpolation provides more interpretable behavior. The
CRBBB case is instructive: zero-masking produced the appear￾ance of external pathway failure (PTB-XL ASS−0.023Z
), but
the primary operator reveals robust external pathway speci￾ficity (ASS 0.455L
)—demonstrating that operator selection
is a necessary precondition for pathway-specificity claims.
Standard discrimination metrics (AUROC> 0.98 for all five
diseases) are insufficient for evaluating whether a classifier
uses disease-consistent signal pathways under this audit.

permutation tests and DeLong comparisons reported in
the Results use sample-level inference (n ≈ 69, 500

patients than to the number of ECGs. Patient-clustered

we recommend that readers treat the patient-level boot￾strap CIs (not the permutation p-values) as the primary

other unmodeled dataset characteristics may contribute

10) Limited to 5 cardiac conditions: Many other ECG
diagnoses not evaluated.
11) No cardiologist review: Manual inspection of failure
cases would strengthen clinical interpretation.
12) Hybrid models unexplored: Combining Clinical-MVP
features with learned representations may offer further
improvements.
G. Future Work
Several directions merit further investigation. The cross￾architecture perturbation audit (Section IV-B) has been com￾pleted on CODE-15%; extending it to the external PTB￾XL dataset under linear interpolation would reveal whether
architecture-dependent ASS patterns survive dataset shift.
Validation on additional independent datasets across differ￾ent continents, devices, and populations is needed to es￾tablish generalizability. A dedicated cardiologist-adjudicated
subset of CODE-15% remains important for formal label￾noise quantification. Lead-stratified perturbation experiments
with clinician review of failure cases would add anatomical
granularity beyond the current all-lead protocol. Extending
the audit panel to more diagnoses, incorporating subgroup
and fairness analyses, and evaluating hybrid models that
combine handcrafted features with learned representations
are natural next steps. More realistic perturbation designs—
including physiologically motivated simulations instead of
signal removal—could strengthen mechanistic interpretation.
Finally, the operator-comparison battery findings demonstrate
that perturbation operator choice is an important influence
on pathway conclusions in matched-control audit design; the
broader perturbation literature would benefit from community

studies.
VI. CONCLUSION
We propose a model-agnostic matched-control pathway au￾dit protocol for evaluating pathway-specific evidence in ECG
classifiers. The protocol requires that (i) targeted perturba￾tions are compared against anatomically matched controls,
(ii) the perturbation operator is documented and compared
via a preregistered operator-comparison battery, (iii) path￾way specificity is re-tested under frozen-weight transfer to
an independent cardiologist-validated dataset, and (iv) per￾model evidence tiers—pathway-supported, evidence-limited,
not supported—are assigned to each (architecture, disease)

and external transfer without aggregating across architectures.

evidence. With explicit operator selection and external validation,

thereby provides an evaluation axis that is clinically interpretable

matched-control perturbation, pathway audit, operator compar￾ison, cross-dataset transfer, pathway-specific evidence, patient￾level validation
I. INTRODUCTION
Deep learning classifiers for electrocardiogram (ECG) anal￾ysis now achieve high discrimination across a growing set of
cardiac conditions [1]–[4], aided by large public datasets such
as PTB-XL [5] and CODE-15% [6]. But strong discrimination
does not tell us whether a model relies on disease-relevant
signal regions—a gap that matters for clinical deployment
beyond benchmark performance. A 1AVB classifier might
depend on QRS morphology instead of PR-interval timing; an
AFIB classifier might use ventricular rate irregularity, atrial
waveform features, or unrelated shortcuts. Standard bench￾mark metrics cannot distinguish these cases. Moreover, exist￾ing explanation methods rarely test whether disease-relevant
regions dominate over matched controls, or whether pathway
dependence holds up under dataset shift—sensitivity is not
specificity, and explanation conclusions can be fragile under
distribution shift [7], [8].
We address these gaps with a model-agnostic, matched￾control perturbation audit protocol. For each diagnosis we
pre-specify an expected positive pathway (e.g., the PR-target
window for 1AVB, the QRS complex for bundle branch block)
and compare targeted perturbations against anatomically adja￾cent control regions that should matter less. A pathway claim
is accepted only if the target perturbation is more disruptive
than its strongest matched control—a stricter criterion than
perturbation sensitivity alone. We further evaluate pathway
specificity under frozen-weight transfer from CODE-15% to

cardiologist-validated PTB-XL fold 10, providing an external
check on whether explanation conclusions are dataset-specific.
The protocol is model-agnostic: the same perturbation design
applies to any classifier accepting 12-lead ECG input, and
the five diseases are a case-study panel chosen to span three
diagnostic pathway categories (timing, morphology, rhythm),
not an exhaustive clinical survey.
We instantiate the matched-control waveform audit across
three raw-signal architectures (ResNet, SE-ResNet, and a
lightweight Transformer). Feature-space XGBoost baselines
(simple summary features and timing-enriched Clinical-MVP
features) provide representation-level context for discrimina￾tion across explicit rhythm, morphology, and timing feature
channels but are not assigned waveform perturbation tiers.
The protocol is evaluated internally on CODE-15% (345,779
exams, patient-level split) and externally on PTB-XL fold 10
(cardiologist-validated labels).
Our primary contribution is the audit protocol itself—a
structured method for evaluating whether ECG classifiers base
decisions on disease-relevant signal regions, rather than on
correlated but clinically non-specific features. We show that
a matched-control design with external transfer can separate
pathway claims that remain anatomically specific and exter￾nally consistent from those that do not, and can identify cases
where target perturbation alone would produce misleading
conclusions. The protocol also reveals that the perturbation
operator itself is a critical methodological variable: zero￾masking, the most common occlusion method in the lit￾erature, creates hard-boundary artifacts that inflate control￾region disruption and can reverse specificity conclusions. A
continuity-preserving operator (linear interpolation) eliminates
this artifact and provides more conservative, anatomically
interpretable ASS estimates. The protocol thus addresses a
gap between standard discrimination benchmarks (which mea￾sure only predictive accuracy) and pathway-specific evidence
(which requires evidence about how models arrive at deci￾sions).
II. RELATED WORK
A. ECG Classification with Deep Learning
1D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and residual
architectures have become the dominant paradigm for auto￾mated ECG classification. Hannun et al. [1] demonstrated
cardiologist-level arrhythmia detection using a 34-layer 1D
CNN on ambulatory ECGs. On the PTB-XL benchmark,
Strodthoff et al. [2] established strong baselines with 1D
ResNets and fully convolutional networks across 71 diagnostic
classes; their follow-up review [3] confirmed that ResNet-style
architectures remain competitive against newer alternatives.
Mehari and Strodthoff [9] further advanced PTB-XL bench￾marks through self-supervised pre-training, while Chen et
al. [10] and Zubair et al. [11] contributed targeted architectures
for multi-class and imbalanced ECG classification.
Beyond vanilla ResNets, SE-ResNet [12] adds channel-wise
attention, and lightweight Transformer adaptations [13] have
been applied via patch-based self-attention. Recent hybrid
architectures combine these paradigms—Cardioformer [14]
couples multi-granularity patching with Transformer layers,
while xECGArch [15] separates morphology and rhythm pro￾cessing with dual CNNs. ECG-JEPA [16] pushed PTB-XL
performance to AUROC=0.945 through JEPA pre-training
on over one million records spanning ten datasets including
CODE-15%. Foundation models such as ECG-FM [17] fur￾ther scale pre-training, though their explanation behavior and
pathway-level auditability remain unexplored. Prior to the deep
learning era, classical machine learning methods—including
XGBoost, random forests, and support vector machines—
were widely applied to handcrafted ECG features and remain
competitive baselines on structured feature sets [18], [19].
Despite these advances across both classical and deep
learning paradigms, the common evaluation framework em￾phasizes discrimination metrics on held-out test splits. It
remains unclear whether these models base their decisions
on disease-relevant signal regions, and whether region-specific
dependence survives cross-dataset transfer. This gap motivates
our multi-level audit protocol, which applies identical pathway
questions across representation levels—from a feature-based
XGBoost baseline to a raw-signal ResNet—allowing us to
assess pathway dependence across both classical and deep
learning models.
B. Explainability and Perturbation Methods
Post-hoc explanation methods—including saliency maps,
occlusion-based sensitivity, guided backpropagation, and in￾tegrated gradients—have been systematically evaluated on
ECG tasks. Storas et al. [20] compared nine gradient-based ˚
methods on synthetic 12-lead ECGs and found that no single
method works best across all measurement tasks, with con￾siderable disagreement between human expert evaluation and
perturbation-based metrics. Suh et al. [21] evaluated eleven
attribution methods across five large ECG datasets and re￾ported that Guided Grad-CAM best aligned with cardiologists’
assessment while localization-based metrics better reflected
human judgment than perturbation-based ones. Plagwitz et
al. [22] assessed the reliability of feature attribution explana￾tions in ECG analysis through systematic perturbation testing,
reporting that explanation reliability varies substantially across
attribution methods and disease categories. Al-Zaiti et al. [23]
found that clinically deployed saliency maps for occlusion
MI detection were rated only slightly clinically relevant by
practicing clinicians, underscoring the gap between current
explanation quality and clinical expectations.
Perturbation-based evaluation—in which input regions are
removed or altered to measure prediction change—provides
a more direct test of feature dependence than gradient-based
attributions alone. Wagner et al. [24] proposed a structured
XAI framework for ECG that combines occlusion-based san￾ity checks, glocal attribution aggregation, and concept-based
analysis, providing quantitative evidence that model behav￾ior can align with cardiologists’ decision rules. Bender et
al. [25] demonstrated that a ResNet trained for 12-lead ECG
classification learns features analogous to clinical diagnostic
criteria including P-wave morphology, QRS duration, and
PR interval. Recent work has also applied wave masking
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 3 / 28>

IEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 3
and reconstruction-based perturbation strategies [26], [27],
and Shapley-value-based ablation [28] to quantify localized
feature importance in ECG classifiers. Beyond ECG, Ross
et al. [29] demonstrated that constraining models to produce
“right” explanations during training can improve generaliza￾tion, providing an alternative to post-hoc auditing—though
their approach requires ground-truth explanation annotations
that are rarely available for clinical ECG tasks.
Despite these advances, three structural limitations persist
across the existing ECG explanation literature. First, existing
perturbation studies rarely incorporate matched anatomical
controls: they test whether a region matters, but not whether
disease-specific regions matter more than adjacent control
regions. This is the key distinction between perturbation
sensitivity (a region is important) and anatomical specificity (a
disease-specific region is more important than its anatomically
adjacent controls)—a distinction we operationalize through the
ASS metric and matched-control design. Second, explanation
conclusions are typically validated only within the training
distribution. Adebayo et al. [7] showed that saliency maps
can fail basic sanity checks under simple input transfor￾mations, Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola [30] demonstrated that
interpretability methods can be fragile under input pertur￾bations, and Ong Ly et al. [31] demonstrated that hidden
data acquisition biases in ECG datasets can inflate model
performance by up to 20%, with AUROC dropping from 0.90
to 0.70 under external validation. In medical imaging more
broadly, DeGrave et al. [32] showed that deep learning models
for radiographic COVID-19 detection selected clinically irrele￾vant shortcuts over meaningful signal—a finding that directly
parallels our concern about ECG classifiers exploiting non￾specific waveform features. Third, few studies test whether
explanation claims survive external dataset shift [8]. These
gaps directly motivate our matched-control perturbation design
with frozen-weight cross-dataset transfer.
C. Dataset Use and Cross-Dataset Validation
The two largest public 12-lead ECG datasets—PTB-XL [5]
(21,837 records, cardiologist-validated labels) and CODE-15%
[6] (345,779 exams, automated labels)—have enabled a wide
range of deep learning studies. PTB-XL provides carefully
annotated multi-label diagnoses with rich metadata including
signal quality indicators and demographic attributes, while
CODE-15% offers an order of magnitude more samples but
with labels derived from an automated interpretation system.
This label-source asymmetry introduces a critical distinction:
models trained on CODE-15% may learn to replicate the
automated labeling logic rather than physician-level diagnostic
features, creating a label circularity risk that varies by disease
category. The PTB-XL+ dataset [33] supplements PTB-XL
with 71 handcrafted features spanning heart rate variability,
QRS morphology, and signal quality metrics, enabling direct
comparisons between learned representations and classical
ECG parameters.
Cross-dataset validation remains underutilized in the ECG
deep learning literature, and where it has been attempted,
the results are sobering. Bickmann et al. [18] benchmarked
time-series versus feature-based methods on PTB-XL but
did not include external validation. Soltanieh et al. [34]
addressed out-of-distribution generalization for self-supervised
ECG representations, showing that dataset shift degrades stan￾dard supervised baselines. Frank et al. [35] reported that
models achieving AUROC>0.90 within-dataset for myocardial
ischemia detection experienced substantial performance drops
across six public ECG databases. At the foundation-model
scale, ECGFounder [36] and recent benchmarking efforts [37]
confirm that cross-domain generalization remains a key chal￾lenge even for large pre-trained models with diverse training
data.
The consistent picture is that external validation across
datasets with different label sources, populations, and acqui￾sition protocols is widely recommended but rarely executed,
and even less often applied to explanation claims. Our study
addresses this gap through frozen-weight transfer from CODE￾15% to cardiologist-validated PTB-XL fold 10, treating the
external dataset as a simultaneous check on both prediction
quality and pathway explanation consistency.
D. Clinical Pathway and Mechanistic Analysis
Clinical ECG interpretation relies on well-defined phys￾iological features: PR interval for atrioventricular conduc￾tion timing, QRS duration and morphology for ventricular
conduction, RR interval regularity for rhythm classification,
and P-wave morphology for atrial activity assessment [38].

I. INTRODUCTION
Deep learning classifiers for electrocardiogram (ECG) anal￾ysis now achieve high discrimination across a growing set of
cardiac conditions [1]–[4], aided by large public datasets such
as PTB-XL [5] and CODE-15% [6]. But strong discrimination
does not tell us whether a model relies on disease-relevant
signal regions—a gap that matters for clinical deployment
beyond benchmark performance. A 1AVB classifier might
depend on QRS morphology instead of PR-interval timing; an
AFIB classifier might use ventricular rate irregularity, atrial
waveform features, or unrelated shortcuts. Standard bench￾mark metrics cannot distinguish these cases. Moreover, exist￾ing explanation methods rarely test whether disease-relevant
regions dominate over matched controls, or whether pathway
dependence holds up under dataset shift—sensitivity is not
specificity, and explanation conclusions can be fragile under
distribution shift [7], [8].

pre-specify an expected positive pathway (e.g., the PR-target
window for 1AVB, the QRS complex for bundle branch block)
and compare targeted perturbations against anatomically adja￾cent control regions that should matter less. A pathway claim
is accepted only if the target perturbation is more disruptive
than its strongest matched control—a stricter criterion than
perturbation sensitivity alone. We further evaluate pathway
specificity under frozen-weight transfer from CODE-15% to

The protocol is model-agnostic: the same perturbation design
applies to any classifier accepting 12-lead ECG input, and
the five diseases are a case-study panel chosen to span three
diagnostic pathway categories (timing, morphology, rhythm),
not an exhaustive clinical survey.
We instantiate the matched-control waveform audit across
three raw-signal architectures (ResNet, SE-ResNet, and a
lightweight Transformer). Feature-space XGBoost baselines
(simple summary features and timing-enriched Clinical-MVP
features) provide representation-level context for discrimina￾tion across explicit rhythm, morphology, and timing feature
channels but are not assigned waveform perturbation tiers.
The protocol is evaluated internally on CODE-15% (345,779
exams, patient-level split) and externally on PTB-XL fold 10
(cardiologist-validated labels).
Our primary contribution is the audit protocol itself—a
structured method for evaluating whether ECG classifiers base
decisions on disease-relevant signal regions, rather than on
correlated but clinically non-specific features. We show that
a matched-control design with external transfer can separate
pathway claims that remain anatomically specific and exter￾nally consistent from those that do not, and can identify cases
where target perturbation alone would produce misleading
conclusions. The protocol also reveals that the perturbation

continuity-preserving operator (linear interpolation) eliminates
this artifact and provides more conservative, anatomically
interpretable ASS estimates. The protocol thus addresses a
gap between standard discrimination benchmarks (which mea￾sure only predictive accuracy) and pathway-specific evidence
(which requires evidence about how models arrive at deci￾sions).
II. RELATED WORK
A. ECG Classification with Deep Learning
1D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and residual
architectures have become the dominant paradigm for auto￾mated ECG classification. Hannun et al. [1] demonstrated
cardiologist-level arrhythmia detection using a 34-layer 1D
CNN on ambulatory ECGs. On the PTB-XL benchmark,
Strodthoff et al. [2] established strong baselines with 1D
ResNets and fully convolutional networks across 71 diagnostic
classes; their follow-up review [3] confirmed that ResNet-style
architectures remain competitive against newer alternatives.
Mehari and Strodthoff [9] further advanced PTB-XL bench￾marks through self-supervised pre-training, while Chen et
al. [10] and Zubair et al. [11] contributed targeted architectures
for multi-class and imbalanced ECG classification.
Beyond vanilla ResNets, SE-ResNet [12] adds channel-wise
attention, and lightweight Transformer adaptations [13] have
been applied via patch-based self-attention. Recent hybrid
architectures combine these paradigms—Cardioformer [14]
couples multi-granularity patching with Transformer layers,
while xECGArch [15] separates morphology and rhythm pro￾cessing with dual CNNs. ECG-JEPA [16] pushed PTB-XL
performance to AUROC=0.945 through JEPA pre-training
on over one million records spanning ten datasets including
CODE-15%. Foundation models such as ECG-FM [17] fur￾ther scale pre-training, though their explanation behavior and
pathway-level auditability remain unexplored. Prior to the deep
learning era, classical machine learning methods—including
XGBoost, random forests, and support vector machines—
were widely applied to handcrafted ECG features and remain
competitive baselines on structured feature sets [18], [19].
Despite these advances across both classical and deep
learning paradigms, the common evaluation framework em￾phasizes discrimination metrics on held-out test splits. It
remains unclear whether these models base their decisions
on disease-relevant signal regions, and whether region-specific
dependence survives cross-dataset transfer. This gap motivates
our multi-level audit protocol, which applies identical pathway
questions across representation levels—from a feature-based
XGBoost baseline to a raw-signal ResNet—allowing us to
assess pathway dependence across both classical and deep
learning models.
B. Explainability and Perturbation Methods
Post-hoc explanation methods—including saliency maps,
occlusion-based sensitivity, guided backpropagation, and in￾tegrated gradients—have been systematically evaluated on
ECG tasks. Storas et al. [20] compared nine gradient-based ˚
methods on synthetic 12-lead ECGs and found that no single
method works best across all measurement tasks, with con￾siderable disagreement between human expert evaluation and
perturbation-based metrics. Suh et al. [21] evaluated eleven
attribution methods across five large ECG datasets and re￾ported that Guided Grad-CAM best aligned with cardiologists’
assessment while localization-based metrics better reflected
human judgment than perturbation-based ones. Plagwitz et
al. [22] assessed the reliability of feature attribution explana￾tions in ECG analysis through systematic perturbation testing,
reporting that explanation reliability varies substantially across
attribution methods and disease categories. Al-Zaiti et al. [23]
found that clinically deployed saliency maps for occlusion

practicing clinicians, underscoring the gap between current
explanation quality and clinical expectations.
Perturbation-based evaluation—in which input regions are
removed or altered to measure prediction change—provides
a more direct test of feature dependence than gradient-based
attributions alone. Wagner et al. [24] proposed a structured
XAI framework for ECG that combines occlusion-based san￾ity checks, glocal attribution aggregation, and concept-based
analysis, providing quantitative evidence that model behav￾ior can align with cardiologists’ decision rules. Bender et
al. [25] demonstrated that a ResNet trained for 12-lead ECG
classification learns features analogous to clinical diagnostic
criteria including P-wave morphology, QRS duration, and
PR interval. Recent work has also applied wave masking
